{{Short description|Type of differentiable manifold}}
{{redirect|Parallelizable|the computer science usage|parallel algorithm}}
In [[mathematics]], a differentiable manifold <math>M</math> of dimension ''n'' is called '''parallelizable'''<ref>{{citation | last1=Bishop|first1=Richard L.|last2=Goldberg|first2=Samuel I.|title=Tensor Analysis on Manifolds|year=1968|publisher=Macmillan|location=New York|page=160}}</ref> if there exist [[Smooth function|smooth]] [[vector field]]s
<math display=block>\{V_1, \ldots,V_n\}</math>
on the manifold, such that at every point <math>p</math> of <math>M</math> the [[tangent vector]]s
<math display=block>\{V_1(p), \ldots, V_n(p)\}</math>
provide a [[Basis of a vector space|basis]] of the [[tangent space]] at <math>p</math>.  Equivalently, the [[tangent bundle]] is a [[trivial bundle]],<ref>{{citation | last1=Milnor|first1=John W.|last2=Stasheff|first2=James D.|title=Characteristic Classes|year=1974|page=15|isbn=0-691-08122-0|publisher=Princeton University Press|series=Annals of Mathematics Studies|volume=76}}</ref> so that the associated [[principal bundle]] of [[frame bundle|linear frames]] has a global section on <math>M.</math>

A particular choice of such a basis of vector fields on <math>M</math> is called a '''[[Parallelization (mathematics)|parallelization]]''' (or an '''absolute parallelism''') of <math>M</math>.

==Examples==
*An example with <math>n = 1</math> is the [[circle]]: we can take ''V''<sub>1</sub> to be the unit tangent vector field, say pointing in the anti-clockwise direction. The [[torus]] of dimension <math>n</math> is also parallelizable, as can be seen by expressing it as a [[cartesian product]] of circles. For example, take <math>n = 2,</math> and construct a torus from a square of [[graph paper]] with opposite edges glued together, to get an idea of the two tangent directions at each point.  More generally, every [[Lie group]] ''G'' is parallelizable, since a basis for the tangent space at the [[identity element]] can be moved around by the action of the translation group of ''G'' on ''G'' (every translation is a diffeomorphism and therefore these translations induce linear isomorphisms between tangent spaces of points in ''G'').
*A classical problem was to determine which of the [[sphere]]s ''S''<sup>''n''</sup> are parallelizable. The zero-dimensional case ''S''<sup>0</sup> is trivially parallelizable. The case ''S''<sup>1</sup> is the circle, which is parallelizable as has already been explained. The [[hairy ball theorem]] shows that ''S''<sup>2</sup> is not parallelizable. However ''S''<sup>3</sup> is parallelizable, since it is the Lie group [[SU(2)]]. The only other parallelizable sphere is ''S''<sup>7</sup>; this was proved in 1958, by [[Friedrich Hirzebruch]], [[Michel Kervaire]], and by [[Raoul Bott]] and [[John Milnor]], in independent work. The parallelizable spheres correspond precisely to elements of unit norm in the [[normed division algebra]]s of the real numbers, complex numbers, [[quaternion]]s, and [[octonion]]s, which allows one to construct a parallelism for each. Proving that other spheres are not parallelizable is more difficult, and requires [[algebraic topology]].
*The product of parallelizable [[manifold]]s is parallelizable.
*Every [[Orientability|orientable]] [[Closed manifold|closed]] [[3-manifold|three-dimensional manifold]] is parallelizable.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Benedetti|first1=Riccardo|last2=Lisca|first2=Paolo|date=2019-07-23|title=Framing 3-manifolds with bare hands|url=https://www.ems-ph.org/doi/10.4171/LEM/64-3/4-9|journal=L'Enseignement Mathématique|language=en|volume=64|issue=3|pages=395–413|arxiv=1806.04991|doi=10.4171/LEM/64-3/4-9|s2cid=119711633|issn=0013-8584}}</ref>

==Remarks==
*Any parallelizable [[manifold]] is [[Orientability|orientable]].
*The term ''[[framed manifold]]'' (occasionally ''[[rigged manifold]]'') is most usually applied to an embedded manifold with a given trivialisation of the [[normal bundle]], and also for an abstract (that is, non-embedded) manifold with a given stable trivialisation of the [[tangent bundle]].
*A related notion is the concept of a '''π-manifold'''.<ref>{{citation | last1=Milnor|first1=John W. |title=Differentiable manifolds which are homotopy spheres|year=1958|url=https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/homsph.pdf}}</ref> A smooth manifold <math>M</math> is called a [[π-manifold]] if, when embedded in a high dimensional euclidean space, its normal bundle is trivial. In particular, every parallelizable manifold is a π-manifold.
